items.context: PII regex patterns (especially email and IP address) will match false positives in Go source code. Email patterns match import paths like 'user@v2', IP patterns match version strings like '1.2.3.4'. The research identified this risk but deferred the mitigation approach.

options.label: Context-aware line filtering
options.rationale: Skip matches inside import blocks, build tags, go.mod/go.sum, and common false-positive contexts (URLs, version strings). Implemented as a post-match filter function. More precise but adds complexity to the scanner.

options.label: File-extension and path-based filtering only
options.rationale: Only scan files with extensions likely to contain real PII (.env, .yaml, .json, .md, .txt, .csv) and skip .go/.ts source files for PII patterns. Simpler but misses PII in source code comments and string literals.

options.label: Rely on allowlist system for tuning
options.rationale: Ship all patterns as-is and let users create allowlist rules for false-positive paths. Simplest implementation but poor out-of-box experience — users get flooded with false positives initially.

items.context: The watchlist stores user-provided PII values encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The key must be available at runtime. The research specified an env var approach but didn't name the variable or define behavior when the key is absent.

options.label: Required env var, fail-fast on startup
options.rationale: Env var `WATCHLIST_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (32-byte hex). If missing, secrets-manager refuses to start. Simplest and safest — no risk of accidentally storing plaintext. But blocks startup if watchlist isn't needed yet.

options.label: Optional env var, watchlist endpoints disabled when absent
options.rationale: If `WATCHLIST_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is not set, watchlist CRUD returns 503 and scan-files ignores the watchlist option. PII and secrets scanning still work. Scan-files response includes a `watchlist_available: false` field. Allows gradual adoption without blocking core functionality.

options.label: Auto-generate and persist key on first use
options.rationale: Generate a random key on first watchlist creation, store it in a local file or DB. Convenient but introduces key management complexity and makes backup/restore harder.

items.topic: Default allowlist rules for common false-positive paths
items.context: Test files, fixtures, and vendored dependencies are common false-positive sources for PII detection. We can ship pre-configured allowlist rules that users can disable/modify, or start with an empty allowlist.

options.label: Ship with sensible defaults, user can disable
options.rationale: Pre-seed allowlist with rules for `*_test.go`, `testdata/**`, `**/fixtures/**`, `**/vendor/**`, `go.sum`, `package-lock.json`. Mark as enabled by default. Provides good out-of-box experience and reduces initial noise. Users can disable or modify.

options.label: Empty allowlist, user configures everything
options.rationale: Start clean. Users add rules as needed. Ensures no surprises but poor initial experience — every test file triggers findings.

items.context: Custom watchlist values need to be matched against file contents. The research says 'literal/substring matching, not regex compilation'. But there's a question of how to handle partial matches and case sensitivity.

options.label: Case-insensitive substring match
options.rationale: Use `strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(line), strings.ToLower(value))`. Catches variations like 'Matt@Example.com' matching 'matt@example.com'. More findings, some may be noisy for path-type values.

options.label: Case-sensitive exact substring match
options.rationale: Use `strings.Contains(line, value)`. Precise but misses case variations. Users must add multiple entries for different casings.

options.label: Per-entry configurable (case-sensitive flag on each watchlist entry)
options.rationale: Add `case_sensitive BOOLEAN DEFAULT false` to the watchlist table. Maximum flexibility but more complex CRUD UI and schema.

items.text: The existing `security_scan_runs` and `security_vulnerabilities` tables fully support the scan-run model needed for file-list scanning. The `persistSecurityScan()` function handles fingerprint dedup and regression detection. No schema changes needed for these tables — only the two new tables (pii_watchlist, scan_allowlist_rules) require migration.
